ox: Correct. The question asks only for the mean (average) reduction, so use only the two means from the Hypertrol row: 139.2 at baseline and 123.4 at 8 weeks. 139.2 − 123.4 = 15.8 mmHg.
Incorrect. 16.8 is one mmHg too large. It comes from a borrowing mistake when subtracting 123.4 from 139.2; the correct difference is 15.8.
Incorrect. 17.8 does not match 139.2 − 123.4. It is two mmHg too large and is not supported by any value in the table.
Incorrect. 18.8 does not match the table either. The standard deviations (11.9 and 10.5) are not part of the reduction and should not be added in.

concept.t: Reading and subtracting means from a results table
p: 'Mean reduction' means baseline mean minus follow-up mean for the treated group. Ignore SDs (spread) and the placebo row unless the question asks for a comparison.

bp968_0.trap: The standard deviations tempt you to use them in the calculation; the reduction uses only the means.
bp968_0.eli: Reduction is just 'how much lower did the average get': start number minus end number.
mem: Mean reduction = baseline mean − follow-up mean.
SD tells spread, not change.
Use the row for the group in the question (Hypertrol, not placebo).

fm.f: Mean reduction = baseline mean − 8-week mean, where baseline mean = Hypertrol group's average SBP at the start, 8-week mean = average SBP after 8 weeks
fm.why: The question asks how far the average fell, so we subtract the end average from the start average.

ox: Correct. High CO2, high H+ (lower pH) in active muscle lowers Hb's affinity for O2 (Bohr effect), so the curve shifts right and more O2 is released.
Wrong. Cooler temperature increases affinity and shifts the curve left. Trap: forgetting heat shifts right.
Wrong. Fetal Hb binds O2 more tightly than adult Hb, shifting the curve left so it can take O2 from mom. Trap: thinking fetal Hb unloads easily.
Wrong. CO binds Hb strongly and also makes remaining O2 bind more tightly, shifting left. Trap: assuming a poison lowers affinity.

p: The oxyhemoglobin curve shows how full Hb is with O2 at different O2 pressures. A right shift means Hb lets go of O2 more easily (lower affinity). A left shift means Hb holds O2 tighter.
Right shift: more CO2, more H+ (lower pH), higher temperature, more 2,3-BPG. These happen in working muscle, which needs more O2.

q34.eli: Hot, busy muscles call out for oxygen, so the delivery truck drops off its cargo more easily.
mem: Right shift: high CO2, H+, temperature, 2,3-BPG
Left shift: opposites, plus fetal Hb and CO
Right shift = lower affinity = more unloading
q34.mn: CADET face Right: CO2, Acid, 2,3-BPG (DPG), Exercise, Temperature all shift the curve right.
q34.trap: Mixing up which direction means higher affinity. Right = release.
q34.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (biochemistry/physiology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Aldosterone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct to keep Na+ and excrete K+. Water follows Na+, raising blood volume.
Wrong. Inserting aquaporins to reabsorb water is ADH. Trap: mixing up the two hormones.
Wrong. Decreasing Na+ reabsorption is ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide). Aldosterone does the opposite. Trap: reversing the direction.
Wrong. Glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, mostly by transporters, not by aldosterone. Trap: picking the wrong segment.

p: Aldosterone is a steroid hormone from the adrenal cortex. It acts in the distal tubule and collecting duct. It makes cells reabsorb sodium (Na+) and secrete potassium (K+).
Water follows sodium by osmosis, so blood volume and pressure rise. The renin-angiotensin system triggers aldosterone release when pressure is low.

q35.eli: Aldosterone is a salt-saver. It tells the kidney to keep salt and water in the body.
mem: Aldosterone: Na+ in, K+ out, water follows
ADH: water only, via aquaporins
ANP: opposite of aldosterone
q35.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (physiology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. Pepsin is the stomach protease, made from pepsinogen. It does not activate trypsinogen. Trap: choosing the most famous protease.
Correct. Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) on the duodenal lining cuts trypsinogen into active trypsin. Trypsin then activates other pancreatic zymogens.
Wrong. HCl activates pepsinogen to pepsin in the stomach, not trypsinogen. Trap: mixing up the two activations.
Wrong. Bile salts emulsify fats, breaking large drops into small ones. They do not cut proteins. Trap: confusing digestive helpers.

p: Pancreatic enzymes are made as inactive precursors called zymogens, so they do not digest the pancreas itself. Trypsinogen is one.
In the duodenum (first part of the small intestine), enteropeptidase cuts trypsinogen to trypsin. Trypsin then activates more trypsinogen and other zymogens (chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase).

q36.eli: A safety cap keeps a tool locked. A key in the intestine unlocks the first tool, and that tool unlocks the rest.
mem: Enteropeptidase: trypsinogen to trypsin
Trypsin activates the other zymogens
HCl activates pepsinogen in the stomach
q36.trap: Choosing pepsin or HCl because they are the stomach's famous activators.
q36.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (physiology/biochemistry texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. Helper T cells release cytokines that direct B cells and others, but they do not make antibodies. Trap: confusing coordinating with producing.
Correct. Plasma cells are activated B cells that make and secrete large amounts of antibodies.
Wrong. Macrophages eat pathogens and show antigens to T cells. They do not secrete antibodies. Trap: assuming all immune cells do all jobs.
Wrong. NK cells kill infected or tumor cells directly, without antibodies. Trap: mixing innate and adaptive cells.

p: B cells are white blood cells of the adaptive immune system. When a B cell meets its antigen (a molecule it recognizes), often with help from helper T cells, it becomes a plasma cell.
Plasma cells are antibody factories. Antibodies are proteins that bind specific antigens. Some B cells become memory B cells for future infections.

q37.eli: A B cell is a recruit who learns the enemy's face. A plasma cell is the factory that mass-produces wanted posters for that face.
mem: Plasma cell = secreting B cell
Helper T (CD4) = coordinate
Cytotoxic T (CD8) and NK = kill cells directly
q37.trap: Picking helper T cells because they are called the 'conductors' of the response.
q37.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (immunology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Wrong. The stomach mostly churns and starts digesting protein. Only alcohol and a few drugs cross its wall well. Trap: thinking digestion and absorption happen in the same place.
Correct. The small intestine is lined with folds, villi and tiny microvilli, which create a huge surface area. Sugars, amino acids, fats, vitamins and minerals are absorbed here.
Wrong. The large intestine mainly takes back water and electrolytes and holds waste. Trap: picking the 'last stop' because it feels like the final step.
Wrong. The esophagus is only a tube that moves food by peristalsis (wave-like squeezing). Nothing is absorbed there.

p: Digestion means breaking food into small pieces. Absorption means moving those pieces into the blood or lymph. Most absorption happens in the small intestine.
Its wall has villi (finger-like folds) covered in microvilli (tiny hairs on each cell). These make a very large surface area, so nutrients pass into the body quickly.

q38.eli: A paper towel with lots of folds soaks up more water than a flat sheet. The villi are the folds.
mem: Small intestine = main site of nutrient absorption
Villi and microvilli = more surface area
Large intestine = water and electrolytes
Stomach absorbs almost nothing (alcohol, some drugs)
q38.trap: Do not confuse where digestion starts (mouth, stomach) with where absorption mostly happens (small intestine).
q38.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (biology/physiology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.

ox: Correct. Ca2+ binds troponin C. Troponin then shifts tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin, so myosin heads can attach and cross-bridge cycling starts.
Wrong. Ca2+ does not bind skeletal myosin heads. Myosin binds actin and ATP. Trap: assuming calcium acts on the 'motor' directly.
Wrong. Ca2+ does not bind actin itself. It acts through the troponin-tropomyosin complex that sits on actin. Trap: skipping the middle step.
Wrong. Calmodulin is the Ca2+ sensor in smooth muscle, where it activates myosin light-chain kinase. Skeletal muscle uses troponin. Trap: mixing up muscle types.

concept.t: Calcium and troponin in skeletal muscle
p: Actin is the thin filament. At rest, a rod called tropomyosin covers the spots where myosin (the motor protein) would grab actin. Troponin is a protein attached to tropomyosin.
When a nerve signal makes the sarcoplasmic reticulum release Ca2+, Ca2+ binds troponin. The rod moves aside, the spots open, and myosin can bind and pull.

q39.eli: Tropomyosin is a gate cover over the handholds on a climbing wall. Calcium is the key that moves the cover so climbers (myosin) can grab on.
mem: Skeletal: Ca2+ binds troponin, tropomyosin moves
Smooth: Ca2+ binds calmodulin
ATP binding releases myosin from actin; Pi release drives the power stroke
q39.trap: Skeletal muscle uses troponin; calmodulin belongs to smooth muscle. Also, calcium never binds myosin or actin directly.
q39.academic: Written from standard MCAT/textbook knowledge (biology/physiology texts); not checked against a live AAMC document.
